Series::traverse_put_¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::traverse_put_(pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<ExtractSpec> specs, const Series& values) -> Series&

What It Does¶

Writes into the current series through a selector that must stay view-representable, mutates in place, and returns *this.

This is the write-side companion to traverse_slice(). It accepts dynamic selector syntax, but only the subset that can still be lowered into ordinary view operations such as select(), slice(), and unsqueeze().

That restriction is not a limitation by accident. It is the reason to use the method at all. traverse_put_() gives you selector-based writes while still guarding against drifting into masked or gathered writes that would need materialized destination positions.

Parameters¶

specs (pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<ExtractSpec>)

The destination selector.

Accepted selector forms are the same view-representable subset used by traverse_slice():

  • scalar indices

  • positive-step slices

  • SliceAll()

  • Ellipsis()

  • NewAxis()

Rejected selectors include:

  • negative-step slices

  • bool masks

  • integer advanced index series

  • any mixed selector that requires materialized advanced indexing

NewAxis() is still legal because it is only shape bookkeeping.

values (const Series&)

The source values to write into the selected destination region.

Two value modes are accepted:

  • scalar source: broadcast across every selected destination element

  • non-scalar source: element count must exactly match the selected destination element count

As on the other write surfaces, dtype and platform are normalized before the assignment happens.

Returns¶

Series& The same series, after mutation.

Examples¶

Example 1. Shared setup. Start from a simple 3 x 4 grid.

auto grid = pluss::make_series(
    {10.0, 11.0, 12.0, 13.0,
     20.0, 21.0, 22.0, 23.0,
     30.0, 31.0, 32.0, 33.0},
    {3, 4});

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[10, 11, 12, 13],
  [20, 21, 22, 23],
  [30, 31, 32, 33]]

Example 2. A whole-column write is accepted because the destination is plainly view-representable.

const auto middle_column = std::vector<ExtractSpec>{
    pluss::Slicing::SliceAll(),
    std::int64_t{1}};

grid.traverse_put_(
    pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<ExtractSpec>(middle_column),
    pluss::make_series({100.0, 200.0, 300.0}, {3}));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[10, 100, 12, 13],
  [20, 200, 22, 23],
  [30, 300, 32, 33]]

Example 3. NewAxis() is accepted here too. It does not create a new writable destination axis; it only participates in selector normalization.

const auto with_newaxis = std::vector<ExtractSpec>{
    pluss::Slicing::NewAxis(),
    pluss::Slicing::SliceAll(),
    std::int64_t{0}};

grid.traverse_put_(
    pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<ExtractSpec>(with_newaxis),
    pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}, {3}));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 100, 12, 13],
  [2, 200, 22, 23],
  [3, 300, 32, 33]]

Example 4. Scalar broadcast still works after the stricter selector gate has accepted the destination.

const auto row_tail = std::vector<ExtractSpec>{
    std::int64_t{2},
    pluss::Slicing::SliceRange(2, 4, 1)};

grid.traverse_put_(
    pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<ExtractSpec>(row_tail),
    pluss::make_series(-5.0));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 100, 12, 13],
  [2, 200, 22, 23],
  [3, 300, -5, -5]]

Example 5. Reverse slices are rejected even though the broader extract_put_() surface could handle them.

try {
  const auto reverse_specs = std::vector<ExtractSpec>{
      pluss::Slicing::SliceAll(),
      pluss::Slicing::SliceRange(-1, pluss::Slicing::Slice::kUnbounded, -1)};

  grid.traverse_put_(
      pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<ExtractSpec>(reverse_specs),
      pluss::make_series(0.0));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

Series::traverse_put_: selector is not view-representable; use extract() or extract_put_() for materializing paths

Example 6. Bool masks are rejected for the same reason: they require materialized destination positions rather than plain traversal.

try {
  auto row_mask = pluss::make_series({true, false, true}, {3});
  const auto mask_specs = std::vector<ExtractSpec>{
      row_mask,
      pluss::Slicing::SliceAll()};

  grid.traverse_put_(
      pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<ExtractSpec>(mask_specs),
      pluss::make_series(0.0));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

Series::traverse_put_: selector is not view-representable; use extract() or extract_put_() for materializing paths

Notes¶

  • traverse_put_() is the strictest selector-write method on Series.

  • Use it when selector-based writes should stay in the same ordinary traversal/view lane as traverse_slice().

  • If the selector needs masks, reverse steps, or explicit advanced indexing, move to extract_put_().

  • If you want value semantics instead of mutation, use traverse_put().

See Also¶

  • Series::traverse_put: copy-returning sibling with the same selector gate.

  • Series::traverse_slice: read-side companion.

  • Series::extract_put_: broader write surface that accepts materializing selectors.
